analysis.one_liner: Cancels what Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac owe Treasury and releases the companies from government control.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Financial Services Committee without a vote, backed only by its sponsor and two cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Since the 2008 financial crisis, the government has run Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac under a deal that sends their profits to the Treasury in exchange for the rescue the companies received. This bill would declare that debt repaid, end the profit sweep, and let the companies keep their earnings to rebuild their own capital. Once each company held capital equal to 5% of its assets, it would be released from government control.
analysis.who_benefits: Private holders of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac stock — including hedge funds and other investors who bought shares cheaply after the 2008 bailout and had pushed for exactly this outcome — would gain the most. Their shares would jump in value once Treasury's senior claim was wiped out, the profit sweep ended, and the companies were released from government control. Homebuyers and mortgage borrowers might see marginal benefits if the companies returned to private operation, but the bill did not require any of the recovered value to flow to them.

how_it_helps.text: The bill deems Treasury's senior preferred stock in each company repaid in full, redeeming it and terminating the 2008 rescue agreement — erasing a claim worth tens of billions of dollars that Treasury held against the companies.

It requires that, until a company is fully capitalized, all of its net income be retained as capital reserves rather than swept to Treasury or paid out, allowing private shareholders to benefit as the companies rebuild value.
It orders FHFA to terminate the conservatorship of each company once it holds capital equal to 5% of its risk-weighted assets, returning them to private control.

It gives anyone aggrieved by FHFA or Treasury actions a right to sue in federal court for injunctions, with taxpayers covering the legal fees of plaintiffs who win — a mechanism tailored to shareholder lawsuits over the profit sweep.
It bars Treasury from requiring the companies to pay a periodic commitment fee under the rescue agreement.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who forfeit Treasury's senior claim against the companies — a major asset built from the 2008 rescue — and lose future profit sweeps. Affordable housing programs also pay: contributions to the Housing Trust Fund and Capital Magnet Fund would be suspended until each company is fully capitalized, delaying funding for affordable housing construction. If a company were released with thin capital and failed in a future housing downturn, taxpayers could be on the hook for another rescue.

drawbacks.text: Wiping out Treasury's senior preferred claim hands a public asset to private shareholders: the same stockholders whose shares were subordinated in the 2008 rescue would see Treasury's tens-of-billions claim deemed repaid for nothing.

The bill suspends contributions to the Housing Trust Fund and Capital Magnet Fund — the affordable-housing funding streams created in 2008 — until each company reaches 10% capital, which could take years.

Releasing the companies once they hold just 5% capital leaves them thinly cushioned; a bill aimed at preventing another bailout could instead recreate the conditions for one, since the companies' mortgage guarantees carry an implicit federal backstop.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow quickly and directly to a small set of private investors, while the costs — the forfeited Treasury claim and the deferred affordable-housing funding — fall on everyone. The strongest case for the bill was that ending the profit sweep would let the companies rebuild capital and end the limbo of indefinite conservatorship. But the bill cancels Treasury's claim first and sets the release bar low, so the public absorbs the losses up front while shareholders capture the recovery.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never scheduled it for action, and it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Mick Mulvaney introduced the bill on April 12, 2016, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day.
Two House Republicans signed on as cosponsors; no other members of either chamber did.
No further action was ever taken — the committee never held a markup or a vote, and the bill expired with the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, taxpayers kept Treasury's senior claim and the profit sweep from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, and affordable-housing funding was not interrupted. GSE shareholders got nothing.

for.name: Rep. Mick Mulvaney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cancel Treasury's claims on Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and end their conservatorships.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired the bill's fate
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or vote; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only three Republicans sponsored or cosponsored the bill and no chamber ever voted on it, so no party split is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac private shareholders (hedge funds and other investors)
industries.note: The bill wipes out Treasury's senior claim, ends the profit sweep, and releases the companies at 5% capital — the 'recap and release' outcome GSE shareholders had sought. Every dollar of shareholder gain comes from value the Treasury claim and profit sweep otherwise preserved for the public.

industries.industry: Affordable housing programs (Housing Trust Fund and Capital Magnet Fund)
industries.note: The bill suspends the companies' contributions to these funds until each is fully capitalized, delaying money that finances affordable housing for low-income families.
